rv.q: Audiences walk in braced for a dusty museum piece – “expect[ing] to be patiently bored”, as Eliot wrote – and are startled by jolts of modernity, moments of biting satire.
I can pretty much guarantee that you won’t see anything as strange, challenging and fascinating on a London stage this year.

Littler makes full use of the church’s gothic scale and dimensions – including the pulpit – to create an awed sense of strangeness that lends weight to the liturgical rhythm and gravitas of Eliot’s language.
It's Tom Littler's hugely inventive production that really draws us into this version.
If everything in churches were as dramatic and atmospheric as this, Becket’s current successor would not have to worry about declining congregations.
Either way, Eliot was not much of a playwright and this is more arcane, tortured hagiography than it is tragedy.

Murder in the Cathedral isn’t just a history play: its complex arguments about the dangers of doing the right thing for the wrong reason, and about humanity’s desire to shy away from confronting reality are held beautifully up to the light by this luminous production.
This timely revival of a challenging drama is a powerful tour de force.
Littler’s Murder in the Cathedral takes an already beautiful text and then knocks it out of the park in all aspects of the production.
This production exploits its surroundings to the full, and the strong cast delivers a haunting, resonant performance.
This production gives it plenty of life.
It's a night to remember for a long time, though. Travelling on to Theatre Royal Bath it won't have quite the church setting, but it's worth the trip. And Suchet is a marvel.
Deeply atmospheric and moving, this is an unmissable production – spearheaded by Suchet’s mesmerising performance – that follows you long into the night.

cn.t: Critics praise this atmospheric church staging of Eliot's verse drama, with Suchet delivering a commanding performance as Becket. While the dense, oratorio-like text proves challenging, the site-specific production brings welcome life to a rarely revived work.
